indicatorJudgements.rationale: A registration is the output of acting through a formal legal channel, so it is a downstream outcome and not a direct measure of capacity; filing it C overstates it. It reads legal infrastructure, formalisation incentives and tax-driven shell entities as well as intention, and it misses informal activity where the formal channel is weak.

Registration time describes how the state's process enables action, so it is an institutional input and not the capability of people to act. It measures a de jure path for a standard case, and its retirement in favour of the B-READY row is correct.

This scores the institutional channel through which an intention becomes a legal entity, which is an enabling input and not observed action, though I value it as a record of state administrative capacity. It covers one narrow act, its coverage of 82 of 135 countries is a real limit, and digital registries likely bring some income signal.

A count of steps is a legal-design input, and a value frozen at 2019 cannot show whether the institution has changed since. Fewer steps are not always better institutions, because a procedure can be a useful safeguard, and the note's claim of no income signal is too strong since procedure counts probably fall with income.

A completed digital task is an observed act, but it reads general digital participation more than turning an intention into action, and it depends on connectivity and device ownership that follow income. The self-reports and the changing task list also weaken comparability, so it should not be filed as C.

The filing as P is correct: this names the construct directly as a feeling, but a person can feel in control without any institution that lets the intention be carried out. Response styles differ across cultures and I do not know how far they distort the country comparison, so my validity judgement is uncertain.

It counts only intentions that end in a limited liability company, so it is a formal-sector outcome rather than a direct capability measure, and it misses own-account and informal activity in India, Brazil and similar countries. It also reads tax and company-law incentives such as shell registration, and I am unsure how far income drives it once those are separated.

It measures a formal rule environment as written for a standardised firm, which is a condition for action and not action itself, and it says little to people who never register. The retirement is correct, and the frozen 2019 series should stay out.

It scores the cost of the formal gate, so it is an input to agency and not an observation that anyone acted, and it is silent on the majority who act without that gate in many low- and middle-income countries. The missing 53 of 135 countries are not random, and a cost term probably links the score to income, although a score that blends time and cost makes the size of that link hard to know.

A count of official steps on paper is an input and describes a de jure route that informal actors bypass, while a 2019 freeze means it reads an old state of the rules. A step count does avoid money, which lowers the wealth risk but does not raise validity much.

The redefinition counts an act, but attaching a file or using a spreadsheet formula is mainly a precondition for action and is tied to device ownership and office work, so it strongly tracks income. The named tasks also miss mobile-first practice such as mobile money and informal commerce on messaging apps, where grassroots digital agency in poorer countries is most visible.

It is the one row here that reaches people outside the registers, which makes it valuable from my stance even though it observes a feeling and not action. Income and cultural response style both move it, so it should sit beside a behavioural measure and not replace one, and its wide uncertainty should be stated.

A count of registered LLCs is an outcome of formalisation and of a developed legal-corporate infrastructure; rich states and tax-haven style registries (Estonia, Dubai-type regimes) inflate it, while informal action in poorer countries is invisible. It shows that incorporation is cheap and common, not that intentions turn into action.

Registration time is a regulatory friction input to action, not action itself, and it is a stale 2019 series. Digitised registries are bought with state budget, so the variation partly follows income.

A B-READY score measures the de jure and de facto ease of registering a firm, an enabling input rather than a capability to act. Coverage of 82 of 135 skews to countries that joined the exercise, and the blended score hides what drives it; it likely tracks income and e-government spend.
A step count is cheap of income but a frozen 2019 reading of rules on paper, not of whether anyone converts intent into a firm. Fewer steps can mean a lean state or just an absent one.

Counting a person who did a task is closer to action than a skill level, but doing digital tasks follows device access, schooling and income very closely. Self-report, shifting task lists and 33 of 53 countries covered (no US, India, China) make it weak, and it has no data now.

Felt freedom of choice is a perception of agency, not conversion of intent to action, and it is culturally scaled (fatalism and modesty norms differ). It rises with income but less steeply than material measures; no usable open data.

The concept is central to cooperation among strangers, but this composite records reputation among experts and firms and not how rules operate. The note's correlations with control of corruption and with income support its retirement, and observable court records are the right replacement.

This measures reputation for corruption and tracks income closely, so it says little about whether institutions actually constrain public power. Retirement is right, and audit and prosecution records would serve better, although they also need care because prosecution counts can rise with enforcement.

Days to payment show the performance of the courts as an outcome, and that performance is what lets strangers contract with each other. It measured a stylised case through expert estimates and not through case records, so the filing as C was too generous, and its archived source makes the retirement sound.

Reliable, affordable enforcement is the institutional base of cooperation beyond personal ties, which makes this the row I value most for this dimension. It reports court performance and does not count cooperation itself, so it is O and not C, and the note's phrase court throughput overstates a score built from expert and firm responses that does not read case records.

The firm reports its own encounter with the state, so this observes whether rules hold for a stranger without relying on reputation. It reads the public-facing bureaucracy more than general cooperation, and reticence may make values lowest where fear is highest, so the low end needs care.

Whether the state obeys rulings it loses tests the core institutional guarantee behind trust in rules, and it holds up as a judgement of a specific public act. It reads democracy closely and shares a lineage with the retired WGI rule of law, and a state that seldom loses in its own courts can read high, so it measures judicial constraint more than cooperation among citizens.

Homicide reflects organised crime and policing capacity far more than cooperation beyond personal networks, and a physically safe society can still trust very little. The diagnostic in the note shows it carried wealth into the dimension, so its retirement is correct.

This asks the attitude that the dimension is about, but it is an attitude and not cooperation in practice, and respondents can define most people as their own circle. I treat it as evidence of what institutions produce and not as a capability that exists without them.

I want to care about confidence in institutions, but the note's finding that the battery read higher in closed and electoral autocracies than in democracies suggests that it records deference as much as earned trust. It rewards a court that cannot rule against the state, so the gap should stay open until a measure separates the two.

Naming the stranger makes this the closest question to the dimension, but the name cooperation overstates it because the item asks about stated trust and observes no cooperative act. It is P, and I am unsure how much it overlaps generalised trust across this frame, so the redundancy is a likely overlap and not a measured one.

Administrative records give an observable account of whether a court finishes its work, which is the type of evidence I prefer to opinion. A high rate can reflect quick dismissal or strict filing rules, it says nothing about fairness or compliance, and case definitions differ across publishers, so comparability is a serious unknown.

It is an expert and business perception composite about formal institutions, and the correlations in your note show it mostly repeats income and its sibling composite. It does not see how far cooperation runs through community and customary arrangements, so the retirement is correct.
It measures a reputation among mainly elite and international raters, not corruption or cooperation among strangers. The retirement is correct.

It was an expert estimate for a stylised commercial case, not an observed count of cases, so C overstated it, and it read an institution that supports cooperation rather than cooperation itself. Most exchange in large informal economies never reaches this court, and the retirement stands.

It scores a formal channel for firms, which is an input to cooperation among strangers and not a measure of that cooperation, and your note that it measures throughput rather than opinion should be checked because B-READY mixes expert consultation with firm data. Traders who rely on reputation, associations and mediation are invisible to it, and coverage gaps fall unevenly on poorer countries.

Direct experience of the state as a stranger is the strongest behavioural signal currently scored here, but the survey frame is formal, registered firms, so it misses the street vendor and the household who meet the same officials. Reticence probably differs by regime and income, so I hold this with moderate confidence.

The act is public, but the value is an expert judgement of it, so I refile it from O to P, and it reads constraint on the executive and democracy more than cooperation beyond personal networks. Wealth is a smaller risk here than regime type, and the shared lineage with the WGI estimate means it is not fully independent of what was retired.

Violent death is far downstream of cooperation and is driven by organised crime, and your own diagnostic found it carried income into the dimension. Some low-income places have strong community order, and others that have high homicide still have dense local cooperation, so the retirement is right.

It asks the population directly and so reaches people that formal records miss, but stated low trust can sit beside dense everyday cooperation through rotating savings, kin and neighbourhood networks. The radius of "most people" also varies across cultures, and the item correlates with income in many samples, although I cannot state how much in this frame.

It reads attitudes to the state, not cooperation among strangers, and your own inspection found that it rewards deference in autocracies. People in many countries cooperate well because they route around a state that they distrust, so this row should stay a gap until a measure can separate deference from confidence.

It names the stranger and fits the dimension question better than any other row, but it asks about stated trust and not cooperation, so the name claims more than the item shows. Behaviour-based evidence on grassroots cooperation, for example savings groups and informal credit, would be the better complement if an open source existed for half the frame.

It is record-based, which is a real strength, but it measures court administration among the people who file, and low filing can itself signal that people avoid the courts. A high clearance rate can also come from dismissals, and case mix and reporting capacity differ widely across the frame, so comparability is uncertain.
A perception composite built from rich-country raters and business surveys, with a 0.83 link to log GDP per head. It scores reputation for wealth and order, so rightly retired.
Reputation for corruption, tied to income above 0.9 in practice and correlated with rule of law above 0.95. It measures how a country is seen, not how it behaves.

Days to enforce a contract is a court-throughput outcome, not a direct reading of trust beyond personal networks, and it is a stale 2019 vignette-based series. Faster courts partly reflect judicial budgets.

Mixes time, cost and process quality into one score for a commercial dispute, so it reads court performance for firms. The courts are a result of spending on staff and IT, and 82 of 135 coverage biases the sample; filed C is too generous.

A firm's own experience of a bribe request is behaviour, not reputation, which I credit. But it falls steeply with income and reticence in high-income and closed states biases it, so a low value may mean a cautious answer or a rich state.

Whether the state obeys rulings it loses is a revealed constraint on the strongest party, which is trust in action rather than purchasable. It is expert-coded, correlates 0.88 with electoral democracy, and Singapore-style few-contested-rulings cases can read high.
Driven by organised crime, inequality and policing capacity rather than stranger cooperation, and it added the largest wealth contribution in the model. Correctly disqualified.

The closest direct reading of trust, but a perception and wording- and culture-sensitive; 'most people' can be filled with the respondent's own circle. Income correlation is real but moderate, and Nordic or East Asian highs are not simply bought. No open data.

Confidence in government reads deference in autocracies and satisfaction in democracies, and is adjacent to cooperation beyond personal networks rather than a measure of it. Income link is weak or even negative, which is the problem: it is not capability. No comparable data.
Names the stranger, so it targets the dimension's question better than generalised trust, though it stays a self-report. Moderate income link; carries no data now.

Counted from case records, so it is inspectable, but a clearance rate of 100% also reads a court that rejects or dismisses cases, and capacity follows judicial budgets. Coverage splits between CEPEJ and OECD members, i.e. rich countries only, so it is a wealthy-sample artefact until a second adapter exists.

This composite reads the democratic channel through perceptions and does not ask whether people see themselves in a common project, so retirement is right. Formal accountability still matters to me as an institution, but it belongs elsewhere and counting it here would treat one regime form as the target; the overlap with polarisation is only partial, since both read political contestation.

Tax collection reveals state capacity as much as willingness to fund common goods, so it is a strong institutional fact but only an adjacent one here. Central government scope understates federal states, resource revenue distorts it, and it can come from coercive collection as well as from consent.

The note itself calls this a structural constraint, which is an input or condition and not an outcome of shared purpose, so I correct the filing from O to I. It may shape whether people see a common project, but the causal link is contested, the Gini also reflects policy and data method, and low inequality does not show collective capacity.

Reported membership in the national community is close to the question asked, and the definition properly separates it from pride. It remains a feeling that can exist without any capacity for collective action or any institution to carry it, and an item that reads alike in every regime class may also discriminate little, which I cannot judge without the data.

Giving time to an organisation is a reported behaviour that results from shared commitment and from an organised civil sector, so I file it O and not C. Its meaning changes where state services replace voluntary effort or where volunteering is compelled, and it can reflect individual effort that compensates for institutional failure.

Hostile division does limit a common project, but this expert judgement cannot separate calm between competing camps from calm where no camp may compete, as the note says. Without that separation it rewards suppression of opposition, so it is correct to keep it as a check and not as a score.

Membership in an organisation that acts for strangers shows durable civic organisations, which is the form of collective capacity I trust most, but it is self-reported membership, so I file it O and not C. Membership does not show activity, and legal freedom of association and state-sponsored organisations could affect readings in ways I cannot quantify here.

It reads the formal democratic channel as judged by experts and not whether people see a common project, and much collective action happens outside elections in movements, unions and neighbourhood groups. Pluralism is relevant to the target, but this composite does not observe it at the level of everyday action, so the retirement is correct.

It counts only what the formal tax system captures, so it reads the size of the formal economy and state collection capacity as much as willingness to fund shared goods, and it misses community levies, religious giving and remittances to home towns. Federal structure and resource revenue confound the central-government figure further, so I would remove it from scoring or give it a very low weight.

If kept at all it is a structural condition and closer to I than a downstream outcome in the author's theory, but I file it as O because it is a distributional result of many forces and says nothing direct about imagined common projects. High-inequality countries such as Brazil and South Africa also show strong grassroots solidarity and collective mobilisation, and survey and income concepts differ across countries, so the link is weak in my view.

It is close to the dimension question because it asks whether people count themselves as members, and it does not depend on formal-sector records. It is still a feeling that can coexist with no collective action, and the common project that people imagine may be local or communal and not national, so I keep a wide uncertainty on it.

It is a reported act of contribution and the nearest thing here to direct capability, but "to an organisation" excludes the informal mutual aid that dominates in many low- and middle-income countries. A wording that also captures direct help to neighbours and non-kin would be much stronger, and the self-report and proprietary data limit how far the current figures can be trusted.

An elite-level expert reading of hostile camps is adjacent to the question, and ordinary people can cooperate locally across divides that dominate national politics. The regime artefact is real, so it should stay out of the scores until it can separate calm between camps from enforced calm.

It is a reported behaviour tied to strangers, but belonging to a named charitable organisation is a formal, associational form that favours rich countries with registered non-profit sectors. Excluding religious membership is defensible for measuring religiosity but also removes a main channel of organised giving and mutual aid in many poorer countries, so this row undercounts them.
A perception composite of the democratic channel, which is adjacent to common purpose and not the same thing; Singapore shows the mismatch. Tracks income and Western rater priors. Rightly retired.

Tax take rises sharply with income and state size, and reflects resource rents, federal accounting and coercive collection as much as willingness to fund public goods. A poor country with high voluntary compliance and a rich low-tax one both score wrong.

Disposable-income Gini is a structural condition, not capability for collective action, and unequal places can act together while equal poor ones cannot. Income link is moderate and non-monotonic, and survey vintage varies. Treat as a context check, not a score.

Attachment to the national community fits the question, but it is a self-report prone to deference and nationalism, and it must not be read as capacity to act together. Income link is weaker than most items; no open data.

Time given to organisations is a revealed behaviour that costs the giver and cannot be bought, so it fits a wealth sceptic well. Gallup self-report and informal help outside organisations go unseen, and the data is proprietary so it fails inspection.

Hostile division bears on common-project capacity, and income explains little of it. But the expert rating reads calm in regimes where no opposition may compete, so it needs a design that separates pluralism from suppression. No data now.

Membership in charitable organisations is a reported behaviour that acts for strangers, closer to capability than attitude items. Membership is not activity, answers vary by culture, and rich countries have denser civil-society sectors. Filed C is stretched; the data is not republishable.
